sentences.text: Strigogyps was roughly the size of a large chicken or guan, with a total weight under one kilogram.
The ratio of its wing to leg bone lengths suggests the species was likely flightless.
Its legs were not built for running, indicating a walking lifestyle similar to modern trumpeters.
The type species Strigogyps dubius was described by Gaillard in 1908 based on a single tibiotarsus found in the Quercy phosphorites of France.
The original tibiotarsus of S. dubius was destroyed during the bombing of Munich in World War II, though casts remain.
While other Cariamiformes were mostly carnivorous, Strigogyps sapea likely had a facultatively herbivorous or omnivorous diet.
Strigogyps belongs to the order Cariamiformes and is classified within the family Ameghinornithidae.
Recent studies suggest Strigogyps is a basal member of Cariamae and not closely related to phorusrhachids.
Salmila robusta is considered more basal than Strigogyps, with the clade of Salmila and Cariamae being the sister taxon to Psophiidae within Gruiformes.
Strigogyps fossils date from the Middle Eocene to the Early Oligocene periods and lived in France and Germany during these times.
The animal lived between 48.07 and 33.9 million years ago, from the Lutetian to the Priabonian stages.
It is debated whether fragmentary remains from the Palaeocene and Eocene of England and North America are phorusrhachids, though they are likely not.
